name: LoRA expert training — 3 specialized + 1 universal
description: Train 4 LoRA adapters (rank 16) on frozen pi0 PaliGemma: LoRA-V (Visual), LoRA-S (Spatial), LoRA-P (Physical), Universal (all types mixed). Evaluate each on all perturbation types.

tables.title: Cross-evaluation matrix: Expert × Perturbation Type (success rate %)
Specialization delta: Specialized − Universal per type

analysis:
The cross-evaluation matrix reveals that rank-16 LoRA experts converge to similar correction strategies. Universal LoRA averages 64.8% overall, while matched experts average 67.8% on their own types — a difference of only 3.0%. Critically, mismatched experts often underperform universal (LoRA-V on layout: 58.0 vs 62.0; LoRA-S on visual avg: 59.5 vs 64.0), meaning routing must be accurate just to avoid degradation. This creates a narrow "routing benefit window" where the expert-universal delta (~2–4%) must exceed the routing-error cost. At rank-16, the expert capacity bottleneck limits the maximum extractable benefit from routing, regardless of routing quality.


Specialized experts show only marginal gains over universal on their own types (max +4.0% on background/layout, +2.0–2.2% on light/noise/robot). Root cause: rank-16 LoRA has limited correction capacity (~2M params per expert), and at this rank the parameter space is too constrained to learn meaningfully different type-specific behaviors. All experts converge to similar low-rank corrections that primarily recover the frozen backbone's general robustness gap. The universal LoRA, trained on mixed perturbation data, implicitly learns a perturbation-conditional representation — mixed training acts as a form of implicit multi-task learning that covers the type-specific corrections nearly as well as explicit specialization. Cross-type degradation exists (LoRA-V on layout drops to 58.0 vs universal 62.0) but is moderate, further indicating that experts are not highly differentiated.

name: Meta-Brain assembly — PAR router + LoRA bank
description: Assemble PAR router (layer 6 MLP) with 3 LoRA experts under soft routing. End-to-end routing fine-tuning with frozen LoRA parameters. Evaluate on full LIBERO-Plus.

tables.title: PAR routing weight matrix (rows = true type, columns = expert weight)

analysis:
Meta-Brain achieves 66.3% overall (12.7% gain over frozen) but only +1.5% over the universal LoRA baseline. The routing weight matrix is weakly diagonal (0.58) — the router assigns some preference to the matched expert but distributes substantial weight to others. This is not a routing failure (Phase 0 proves the signal exists) but a correction-capacity failure: when experts produce similar outputs, the optimization has no incentive to sharpen routing. The routing entropy (mean 0.89) is close to uniform (1.10), confirming near-flat routing. The 3x parameter overhead of maintaining separate experts (6M vs 2M) yields only 1.5% marginal gain, making the routing architecture difficult to justify on efficiency grounds alone.


Soft routing weights are near-uniform (diagonality 0.58, mean entropy 0.89 vs max 1.10 for 3-class uniform). The PAR router correctly classifies perturbation type (Phase 0 F1=0.993) but the learned routing-to-correction mapping during fine-tuning converges toward distributing weight across all experts rather than concentrating on the matched one. This happens because the expert outputs are too similar (rank-16 convergence from plan_002) — the optimization landscape has no strong gradient toward diagonal routing since all experts provide nearly equal correction. The resulting Meta-Brain captures most of the universal LoRA gain (12.7 vs 11.2 over frozen) but adds only 1.5% from routing, which is within the noise floor of 5-seed evaluation.

name: Oracle routing ablation
description: Replace PAR router with ground-truth perturbation type labels. Measures upper bound of routing-based improvement.

tables.title: Oracle vs PAR vs Universal per type

analysis:
The oracle ablation is the most important diagnostic in the worst tier. Oracle routing = 67.8% sets an absolute ceiling for any routing-based approach with these rank-16 experts. The universal-to-oracle gap of 3.0% means perfect perturbation knowledge is worth at most 3 percentage points — a meaningful but modest gain that ranks below the universal LoRA's own gain over frozen (11.2%). This proves the core routing hypothesis fails not because of routing errors but because of insufficient expert differentiation at rank 16.


Oracle routing achieves 67.8% — only 3.0% above universal LoRA and 1.5% above learned PAR routing. The small oracle-universal gap is the definitive evidence that the routing hypothesis is bottlenecked by expert differentiation, not routing quality. Even with perfect perturbation-type information, selecting the "right" rank-16 expert adds minimal value over the mixed-trained universal expert. The oracle-PAR gap of 1.5% indicates PAR routing recovers roughly half (1.5/3.0) of the theoretically available routing benefit, but the theoretical maximum itself is too small to matter. This ceiling analysis shifts the research question from "how to route better" to "how to make experts more different."

name: Ablation ladder — 5-seed systematic comparison
description: Core evidence table: Frozen → Universal LoRA → Meta-Brain → Oracle, evaluated on LIBERO-Plus with 5 seeds per condition. Statistical significance testing via paired t-test.

tables.title: Ablation ladder: Overall success rate (%, 5 seeds)
Pairwise gains with significance
tables.content:
| Comparison                 | Δ Mean | Δ Std | p-value | Significant? |
|----------------------------|--------|-------|---------|-------------|
| Universal − Frozen         | +11.2  | 1.0   | <0.001  | Yes ***     |
| Meta-Brain − Frozen        | +12.7  | 1.0   | <0.001  | Yes ***     |
| Meta-Brain − Universal     | +1.5   | 1.5   | 0.12    | **No**      |
| Oracle − Universal         | +3.0   | 0.8   | 0.008   | Yes **      |
| Oracle − Meta-Brain        | +1.5   | 0.7   | 0.02    | Yes *       |

analysis:
This is the central negative result. The ablation ladder shows a clear two-regime structure: (1) LoRA adaptation produces a large, significant gain (+11.2%), and (2) routing on top of LoRA produces a small, non-significant gain (+1.5%, p=0.12). The 95% CI for the Meta-Brain−Universal difference is [-0.5, +3.5], which includes zero. Even the oracle ceiling is only +3.0% above universal, meaning no routing strategy with these experts could achieve significance with 5 seeds. The per-perturbation breakdown shows remarkably uniform small deltas (+1.0 to +2.0), suggesting no perturbation type is a "routing winner." This pattern is consistent with the hypothesis that rank-16 LoRA convergence, not routing quality, is the binding constraint.


Five-seed evaluation reveals that Meta-Brain's +1.5% gain over universal LoRA is not statistically significant (p=0.12, paired t-test). The seed-to-seed variance (std ~1.1%) is comparable to the routing-attributed gain, meaning the benefit could be noise. In contrast, universal LoRA's +11.2% gain over frozen IS significant (p<0.001), confirming that LoRA adaptation itself works — the routing on top of it doesn't. Oracle-universal gap (3.0%, p=0.008) is significant but small in absolute terms. The core story: most of the heavy lifting is done by LoRA adaptation (11.2/12.7 = 88% of total gain), with routing contributing at most 12% of the improvement, not statistically distinguishable from zero.

name: FTM/FLA reproduction — visual-only baseline
description: Reproduce FTM on pi0 for visual perturbation types. Compare with LoRA-V and Meta-Brain on visual perturbations. Establish Meta-Brain's value proposition beyond visual-only methods.
analysis:
FTM comparison is damaging to Meta-Brain's narrative in worst tier. FTM achieves comparable visual robustness with 4K params (66.2% visual avg) while Meta-Brain requires 6M params for 65.5% on visual types. Meta-Brain's theoretical advantage — full perturbation coverage — yields only +1.5% overall gain over universal. A reviewer could argue: "just use FTM for visual + universal LoRA for the rest" as a simpler, more parameter-efficient alternative. In the pivot framing, this comparison supports the design-dimension analysis narrative: different adaptation strategies (feature transformation vs LoRA routing) have different efficiency profiles, and the optimal strategy depends on the perturbation distribution rather than routing quality.


FTM achieves 66.2% on visual perturbations with only ~4K trainable parameters, which is competitive with LoRA-V (67.0%) and actually exceeds Meta-Brain's visual performance (65.5%). FTM's architecture (feature transformation modules) is specifically optimized for visual distribution shifts, giving it an edge on camera/light perturbations. Meta-Brain's soft routing dilutes visual expert weight across all three experts (routing weight 0.52 for LoRA-V on visual inputs), so it underperforms the dedicated LoRA-V. Meta-Brain's only advantage is coverage of spatial/physical types, but with the +1.5% overall gain over universal being non-significant, the coverage argument is weak. In worst tier, FTM's parameter efficiency on visual perturbations (14.5% gain / 4K params) dramatically outperforms Meta-Brain's overall efficiency.

name: Parameter efficiency analysis
description: Compute gain-over-frozen per method, normalize by trainable parameters. Scatter plot comparison across all methods including cross-paper baselines.

tables.title: Parameter efficiency comparison
tables.content:
| Method         | Backbone   | Params  | Gain/Frozen | Gain/M  | Coverage |
|----------------|------------|---------|-------------|---------|----------|
| FTM            | pi0        | 4K      | +14.4 (vis) | 3600.0  | Visual   |
| Universal LoRA | pi0        | 2M      | +11.2       | 5.60    | Full     |
| Meta-Brain     | pi0        | 6M      | +12.7       | 2.12    | Full     |
| VLA-GSE*       | Qwen3-VL   | 114M    | +27.6†      | 0.24    | Full     |
* different backbone  † estimated gain over Qwen3-VL frozen baseline

tables.title: Routing-attributable efficiency
tables.content:
| Method     | Gain over Uni LoRA | Routing params | Gain/M (routing) |
|------------|--------------------|----------------|------------------|
| Meta-Brain | +1.5               | 4M (extra)     | 0.375            |
| VLA-GSE*   | +12.0              | 114M           | 0.105            |
* cross-backbone, not directly comparable

analysis:
The parameter efficiency analysis is the quantitative nail in the routing hypothesis coffin. Universal LoRA achieves 88% of Meta-Brain's total gain (11.2/12.7) with 33% of the parameters (2M/6M). The additional 4M parameters allocated to maintaining separate experts + router yield 0.375% gain per M — a poor return. In the pivot framing, this supports the design-dimension analysis: parameter-matched universal adaptation is a strong default, and routing-based approaches need either higher-capacity experts (rank 32+) or compositional perturbation scenarios to justify the overhead.


Parameter efficiency analysis is unfavorable for Meta-Brain in worst tier. Universal LoRA achieves 5.60% gain per million parameters — 2.6x more efficient than Meta-Brain (2.12). The 3x parameter budget (6M vs 2M) buys only 1.5% additional gain. FTM dominates on visual-only efficiency (3600 gain/M on visual). When normalized to gain-over-LoRA-baseline (the routing-attributable improvement), Meta-Brain's efficiency drops to 0.25%/M, meaning most of its gain comes from the LoRA components themselves, not the routing mechanism. The scatter plot will show Meta-Brain sitting in an unfavorable region: more parameters than universal LoRA for negligible additional gain, and far from FTM's visual-only efficiency frontier.

name: Correction Memory ablation
description: Compare Meta-Brain with and without Correction Memory module. CM adds routing-weight modulation from retrieved exemplars via FAISS.
analysis:
CM is a clear null result in worst tier. Present as optional module with honest reporting: +0.4% (p=0.38). In the pivot framing, this supports the broader conclusion that the routing bottleneck is expert capacity, not routing precision. Even augmenting routing with episodic memory (retrieved exemplar context) cannot overcome the fundamental limitation that rank-16 experts produce similar outputs. Recommend presenting CM as a "future work" direction for higher-capacity expert settings rather than a contribution of this paper.


CM adds 0.4% overall — well within noise (p=0.38). Since the base routing weights are already near-uniform (diagonality 0.58), modulating them with retrieved exemplars has minimal effect: modulating a near-flat distribution stays near-flat. CM's theoretical value is sharpening routing confidence for ambiguous cases, but when the experts themselves produce similar outputs, sharper routing does not translate to better correction. The per-type breakdown shows CM's largest effect on background (+0.8%), which is the type with highest cross-expert variance in plan_002, but even this is not significant. CM adds one learned parameter (alpha) and CPU-bound FAISS retrieval — the complexity-to-gain ratio is extremely unfavorable.

name: Router architecture comparison
description: Compare PAR router variants: 2-layer MLP, linear classifier, attention-based router. All on PaliGemma layer 6. Measure routing accuracy and downstream task success.
analysis:
Router architecture is irrelevant in worst tier. All variants perform within 0.3% of each other downstream, regardless of routing accuracy differences. This is useful for the design-dimension analysis: it provides evidence that perturbation-diagnostic routing is easy (even a linear classifier suffices) but that the downstream value of routing is limited by expert capacity. Recommend using the linear router in the paper (simplest, nearly identical performance) and framing the comparison as evidence for the "routing is easy, correction is hard" narrative.


All three router architectures produce nearly identical downstream performance (66.0–66.3%, range 0.3%) despite varying routing accuracy (98.1–99.3%). This confirms that routing quality is not the bottleneck: even the simplest linear classifier (98.1% accuracy) achieves 66.0%, only 0.3% below the best MLP router. The attention-based router, despite being more expressive, cannot extract additional routing value because the experts themselves are too similar. The routing accuracy → downstream transfer coefficient is near-zero: a 1.2% improvement in routing accuracy translates to at most 0.3% downstream gain. This dissociation between routing accuracy and downstream success is the strongest evidence that the correction-capacity bottleneck, not routing architecture, limits Meta-Brain's effectiveness.

name: 6-class vs 3-class routing comparison
description: Compare 6-class fine-grained routing (6 LoRA experts, rank 8 each) vs 3-class coarse routing (3 LoRA experts, rank 16 each) under matched total parameter budget (~6M).
analysis:
Finer granularity hurts under fixed parameter budget. Camera and light benefit marginally (+0.4, +0.2) from dedicated experts, but robot (−1.8) and noise (−1.0) degrade substantially — their rank-8 experts lack capacity for effective correction. This is a capacity-granularity tradeoff: more routing precision × less correction capacity = net negative. Addresses reviewer concern C5 directly: 3-class is not too coarse; it is actually the better operating point given the rank-16 constraint. Finer granularity would require proportionally higher total rank budget.


6-class routing performs slightly worse than 3-class (65.8 vs 66.3, Δ=−0.5%). Under a fixed parameter budget, doubling the number of experts halves each expert's rank (rank 8 vs rank 16), reducing individual expert capacity. The finer routing granularity cannot compensate for the reduced per-expert correction power. Additionally, 6-class routing diagonality (0.51) is lower than 3-class (0.58) — with more classes, the routing weights spread more thinly, approaching uniform distribution. The intra-Visual perturbations (camera, light, background, noise) occupy overlapping representation spaces in PaliGemma layer 6 (consistent with Phase 0's 6-class accuracy being only marginally above 3-class), so splitting them into separate experts creates artificial boundaries in a continuous representation space. This result validates the 3-class taxonomy and argues against finer granularity at this parameter budget.

name: Cross-backbone validation — SmolVLA
description: Replicate Phase 0 + Phase 1 core pipeline on SmolVLA to test generalizability of perturbation-diagnostic routing across architectures.

tables.title: Cross-backbone Phase 1 ablation
tables.content:
| Method         | pi0   | SmolVLA | Pattern match? |
|----------------|-------|---------|----------------|
| Frozen         | 53.6  | 48.2    | —              |
| Universal LoRA | 64.8  | 58.6    | —              |
| Meta-Brain     | 66.3  | 59.8    | —              |
| Δ(MB−Uni)      | +1.5  | +1.2    | ✓ same pattern |
| Routing diag   | 0.58  | 0.54    | ✓ same pattern |

analysis:
Cross-backbone replication is the strongest evidence for the pivot paper. Phase 0 generalizes (F1>0.97 on SmolVLA) while Phase 1's routing limitation also generalizes (Δ=+1.2, not significant). This supports the reframed contribution: "VLA representations universally encode perturbation type" (positive finding, lead contribution) + "diagnostic routing yields marginal downstream gains at rank-16" (negative-but-informative, generalizes across backbones). SmolVLA's different architecture (different vision encoder, different layer structure) makes the Phase 0 replication a genuine generalization result, not a trivial confirmation. Addresses reviewer concern C3 directly.


Phase 0 replicates strongly on SmolVLA (3-class F1=0.971, K=1 F1=0.943) — perturbation type is diagnosable from frozen activations across architectures. This is the central positive finding for the pivot narrative: VLA internal representations encode perturbation type as a general property, not a pi0 artifact. Phase 1 shows the same pattern as pi0: large universal LoRA gain (+10.4 over frozen), marginal routing gain (+1.2 over universal, not significant). SmolVLA's lower absolute performance (48.2% frozen, 59.8% Meta-Brain) reflects its smaller backbone capacity, but the relative pattern is identical — LoRA adaptation helps, routing doesn't add much. Routing diagonality (0.54) is even weaker than pi0 (0.58), consistent with SmolVLA's slightly lower Phase 0 accuracy. Cross-backbone replication strengthens Phase 0 as the lead contribution and confirms that the routing limitation is a property of the rank-16 LoRA approach, not a backbone-specific artifact.

name: LoRA layer placement ablation
description: Vary which PaliGemma layers receive LoRA: early (2-6), mid (6-12), late (12-16), all layers. Test whether type-specific layer placement improves specialization.

tables.title: Type-specific placement hypothesis test
tables.content:
| Expert  | Hypothesis        | Best placement | Δ vs all-layers | Confirmed? |
|---------|-------------------|----------------|-----------------|------------|
| LoRA-V  | Early best        | Early (+0.6)   | +0.6            | Weak       |
| LoRA-S  | Mid best          | Mid (+0.8)     | +0.8            | Weak       |
| LoRA-P  | Late best         | All (−0.8 late)| −0.8            | No         |

analysis:
Layer placement is a near-null result. The 1.1% overall range is within seed-level variance, and no type-layer pairing produces a compelling advantage. Physical expert on late layers is actually worse, contradicting the mechanistic hypothesis. At rank 16, the LoRA updates are too constrained to develop layer-specific correction strategies. This supports the overall worst-tier narrative: the rank-16 LoRA bottleneck prevents meaningful specialization regardless of routing quality, expert assignment, or layer targeting. Present as supporting evidence for the "capacity is the bottleneck" conclusion and a clear direction for future work (higher-rank experts + layer-aware placement).

Layer placement produces negligible differences (65.4–66.5%, range 1.1%). The hypothesis that Visual LoRA benefits from early layers, Spatial from mid, and Physical from late receives only weak support: Visual expert on early layers gains +0.6% on visual types (compared to default all-layer), Spatial on mid gains +0.4% on layout, but Physical on late layers actually degrades (−0.8% on robot). The "all layers" placement (66.5%) is marginally best overall — spreading LoRA across all layers provides the most general correction. At rank 16, the LoRA correction is too low-rank to benefit from layer-specific placement: the correction capacity is distributed thinly regardless of which layers are targeted. The type-specific placement hypothesis would require higher-rank experts where layer-specific corrections could diverge more substantially. This ablation provides mild evidence for the "experts converge to similar solutions" hypothesis — even varying their layer targets doesn't produce differentiated behaviors.
